messages.author: 36cda290860fb7b2
messages.subject: RE: paired analysis
parts:
Dear List,

I am very new to the field of CNV analysis and aroma package so please
forgive me for naive questions.
I am running the paired analysis as described in tutorial. It seems
that there is a typo in paired analysis code sample, specifically in
"PCR fragment length normalization" instead of:

cesFlnList <- list();
for (chipType in names(csList)) {
ces <- cesCnList[[chipType]];
fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
print(fln);
cesFln <- process(fln, verbose=log);
cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;
}

it should read:

cesFlnList <- list();
for (chipType in names(cesList)) {
ces <- cesList[[chipType]];
fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
print(fln);
cesFln <- process(fln, verbose=log);
cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;
}

otherwise it will not run due to the name mismatch with the previous
("Summarization") section.

After this fix it works and the result of chr.20 for tumor-normal pair
(CRL-5868D, CRL-5957D) is the same as in the vignette,
but I have the difficulty interpreting the results: it seems that big
chunks of output signal (for example, CRL-2324D vs CRL-2325D, chr.
1,2,3)
have a shift of a mean value by a fraction of a unity copy number
relative to each other and I am wondering if this a physical or
processing artifact?
I've learned from the previous discussions on the list that running
tumor sample against the large enough reference set would remove it
through normalization,. but still what process
would cause such a shift in a paired analysis? I thought that
neighboring SNPs are scattered across the chip so it should not be a
local chip luminance variance.
I would greatly appreciate a brief explanation of this phenomenon.

Thank you

Alex Lisovich
University of Pittsburgh, DBMI
200 Meyran Ave

> ces <- cesList[[chipType]];

> cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;

thanks for reporting these typos. The vignette has been updated.

>
> After this fix it works and the result of chr.20 for tumor-normal pair
> (CRL-5868D, CRL-5957D) is the same as in the vignette,
> but I have the difficulty interpreting the results: it seems that big
> chunks of output signal (for example, CRL-2324D vs CRL-2325D, chr.
> 1,2,3)
> have a shift of a mean value by a fraction of a unity copy number
> relative to each other and I am wondering if this a physical or
> processing artifact?

The first and most important comment is that you cannot and should not
interpret the log2 ratios as true/real log2 copy numbers. There are
many reasons for this, but one is that the microarray technology does
not measure the underlying copy number on a linear (proportional)
scale, e.g. if you double the CN the observed signal is not doubled.
What holds is that large CNs have large log-ratios and vice verse.
This comment applies to all CN data sets.

Different methods have been proposed to calibrate the log2 ratios
("raw CNs") toward know CN levels so that can interpret the log2
ratios as true log2 ratios. This kind of calibration can be done
after normalizing the chip effects (e.g. fragment-length
normalization). Doing this kind of calibration will only have little
impact on the segmentation, i.e. you will in practice find the same
breakpoints in both cases (except maybe for some extremely short noise
regions).

I don't know the details about this particular data set, but it is
quite likely that the tumor sample is contaminated by normal cells as
well (very common), which will cause us compare a mixture of tumor and
normals towards normals. That would further explain (true) CN levels
that are not 0, 1, 2, ... Furthermore, if the tumor sample is not
only contaminated by normal cells but also by other kind of tumor
cells that have different CN aberrations, you can get very complicated
regions.

> I've learned from the previous discussions on the list that running
> tumor sample against the large enough reference set would remove it
> through normalization,. but still what process
> would cause such a shift in a paired analysis?

Using a large set of pure normals as a reference is only like have a
single normal sample with very little noise. The more normals you
average over, the less noisy your reference becomes. It does not
affect the CN levels of the reference though. It should reflect CN=2
at all positions (except possibly for common CN polymorphic regions).
Having a small number of normals in the reference will typically just
add noise, but it is unlikely that it will "introduce" CN regions.

> I thought that
> neighboring SNPs are scattered across the chip so it should not be a
> local chip luminance variance.

Each SNP contain multiple probes (except the single CN probes on the
newer arrays). These probes are never placed close to each other.
Instead they are spread out spatially on the array to minimize the
risk that one SNP will be biased by spatial artifacts. Furthermore,
neighboring SNPs on the genome are not placed next to each other on
the array. I don't know if Affymetrix have done a randomization for
this explicitly, but their standard probe position algorithm is likely
to introduce such a "semi-randomization".
> I would greatly appreciate a brief explanation of this phenomenon.

Hope this helps. If not, I suggest that you continue this
non-aroma.affymetrix specific question on Bioconductor where more
people can pitch in.

Cheers

Henrik

messages.author: 36cda290860fb7b2
messages.subject: Re: paired analysis
parts:
Dear Henrik,

Thank you very much for your response, it was extremely useful.
I was thinking that 6 distinctive log2 ratios on CRL-2324D chr.2 is a
bit too much, but the contamination would be a likely explanation.
I would like to ask another question regarding a flow of operation.
Let's suppose I want to use the aroma.affymetrix raw CN estimation to
produce the final CN estimation, then use oligo to produce genotype
calls and then incorporate both CN and genotype calls into the data
structure accessible through some kind of browser, either
ChromosomeExplorer or appropriate BioC package (rtracklayer?)
What would be the strategy to accomplish this? As I understand, oligo
now runs in bounded memory, so both processing pipelines (aroma and
oligo) can be launched on a PC, but we are primarily using a Linux
workstation (32GB +2TB disk space) , so the memory limitations would
not be a problem.

Thank you,

Alex
